content.heading: Building Working-Class Power

children.text: DSA Fort Worth is a member-funded, member-driven organization building working-class power across Tarrant County. Our work is shaped and funded by everyday people and not corporations or wealthy donors. Members help decide our priorities, elect chapter leaders, develop campaigns, and carry out the work necessary to win change.

We organize for economic justice by championing housing, healthcare, strong unions, and public institutions that meet people’s needs. Our politics are anti-imperialist because we believe every person, everywhere, has the right to live a free, humane, and dignified life.

We believe people are capable of making the decisions that affect their workplaces, neighborhoods, communities, and government. By organizing together, we can build a more democratic society and economy that works for everyone.

content.heading: New to DSA Fort Worth? Start Here.

children.text: DSA Fort Worth 101 introduces you to democratic socialism, our chapter, and the work we’re doing across Tarrant County. You’ll learn how DSA operates as a member-led organization, how our chapter makes decisions, and how members and supporters can get involved in campaigns, working groups, committees, events, and political education.
Whether you are ready to join or simply curious about DSA, this session will help you understand who we are and find your place in the chapter.

content.heading: Get Involved, Stay Connected
content.intro: Ready to make a difference in Tarrant County? Below are a few ways you can plug in and get involved.

items.heading: Join DSA
items.body: Become a dues-paying member and help shape the priorities, leadership, and work of your local DSA chapter.

items.heading: Attend an Upcoming Event
items.body: Meet local organizers through campaign actions, political education, chapter meetings, and community events.

items.heading: Find Your Place
items.body: Tell us about your interests, skills, and availability. We’ll help connect you with a campaign, working group, committee, or upcoming opportunity.
items.button_label: Fill Out the Get Involved Form

content.heading: Join the Largest, Socialist Organization in U.S. History

children.text: Our power comes from people choosing to organize together. When you join DSA, you become part of shaping what our chapter does and what we can accomplish across Tarrant County.
As a member of DSA Fort Worth, you can:
Propose new projects and areas of work
Vote on chapter priorities, resolutions, endorsements, and leadership
Help develop campaigns and organizing strategies
Join working groups and committees
Build organizing efforts, communications, research, and leadership skills
Organize alongside people committed to working to build socialism in our community

content.heading: Know What’s Happening. Be Ready to Act.

children.text: Decisions affecting our neighborhoods, workplaces, public resources, and rights can move quickly. Subscribe to the DSA Fort Worth newsletter for local campaign updates, upcoming events, political education, community resources, and opportunities to take action.

items.question: What is DSA?
items.answer: The Democratic Socialists of America is a member-funded, member-led political organization. DSA members organize in their workplaces, communities, and political institutions to build a society and economy that meets people’s needs democratically. [Democratic Socialists of America →](https://www.dsausa.org/)

items.question: What does DSA Fort Worth do?
items.answer: DSA Fort Worth organizes people across Tarrant County through campaigns, working groups, community events, and other forms of collective action. Our priorities and activities are determined by our members.

items.question: How do I join DSA Fort Worth?
items.answer: Join DSA through [go.dsausa.org/fort-worth-f26](https://go.dsausa.org/fort-worth-f26). After joining the national organization, your membership information will be shared with the local chapter through regular membership updates.

data.title: Events
data.lead: DSA Fort Worth hosts campaign actions, political education, chapter meetings, and social events throughout Tarrant County. Whether you are a longtime member or learning about DSA for the first time, our events offer a way to meet local organizers, explore socialist politics, and find your place in the chapter.

children.text: DSA Fort Worth 101 introduces you to democratic socialism, our chapter, and the work we are building across Tarrant County.
During the session, you will learn:
What DSA is and what democratic socialists believe

items.question: Do I have to be a member to attend events?
items.answer: Many DSA Fort Worth events and activities are open to non-members. Certain votes, elections, meetings, and internal activities are limited to members in good standing.

data.title: Our Work
data.lead: DSA Fort Worth members are organizing across Tarrant County. Our chapter’s campaigns and initiatives fight for lasting change in our communities and work to build working-class power.
data.hero_image_brief: Members canvassing a Fort Worth neighborhood

children.text: Campaigns are chapter-wide efforts meant to achieve a specific political or organizing goal. They give members and community supporters a way to transform shared concerns into collective power through research, political education, canvassing, public pressure, coalition work, and direct action.
Our campaigns address immediate conditions while building the relationships, skills, and organizational power needed to fight for a more democratic and socialist future.

items.heading: No More Data Centers in Fort Worth
items.body:
Data centers are expanding across Fort Worth, consuming our water and energy while polluting our environment. DSA Fort Worth is organizing residents to push Fort Worth City Council to adopt a moratorium on new data center developments.

[Sign the petition to demand a stop to new data center development in Fort Worth](https://fortworthdsa.solidarity.tech/stop-data-center-development-in-fort-worth)

[Join an upcoming canvass to take action with DSA](https://fortworthdsa.solidarity.tech/no-data-centers-in-fort-worth-canvass-for-a-moratorium?event_session_ids=97013)

items.heading: Power to the Tenants
items.body: Tenants across Tarrant County are facing rising housing costs, unsafe living conditions, and unresponsive property management. DSA Fort Worth is organizing to build united tenant power across Tarrant County so that working-class people can transform their neighborhoods and communities.

children.text: Our Working Groups are organized around ongoing political issues such as housing, immigrant justice, and electoral power. Working groups provide a lasting home where members can study an issue, develop strategy, and propose campaigns.

items.heading: Housing Working Group
items.body: The Housing Working Group organizes alongside Tarrant Tenants United and local tenant associations to help build a powerful, fighting, and socialist-oriented tenant movement in Tarrant County.

items.heading: Abolish ICE Working Group
items.body: The Abolish ICE Working Group organizes around immigrant rights, detention and deportation, surveillance, political repression, and the broader systems that criminalize immigrant communities.

items.heading: Electoral Working Group
items.body: The Electoral Working Group organizes to build an independent socialist political bloc in local and state government that represents people over profit and advances economic justice, anti-imperialism, and democracy for all.

items.heading: Labor Working Group
items.body: The Labor Working Group works with labor unions, organizes to create new unions, and supports striking workers. We seek to strengthen labor in Tarrant County by merging the militant & socialist currents within the labor movement to build working class power.

children.text: Campaigns and working groups depend on strong internal infrastructure. DSA Fort Worth’s committees provide the communications, education, technology, membership development, and administrative support needed to sustain our organizing.
Committees are open to members who want to contribute their skills, learn something new, and help build an organization capable of winning a better world.

items.heading: Communications and Design Committee
items.body: The Communications and Design Committee shapes how DSA Fort Worth communicates with members, supporters, and the broader public.

items.heading: Growth and Development Committee
items.body: The Growth and Development Committee helps recruit, onboard, and develop members in the chapter. The committee develops the chapter’s recruitment, onboarding, retention, mentorship, community outreach, and fundraising strategies.

items.heading: Political Education Committee
items.body: The Political Education Committee creates accessible opportunities for members to study socialist history, theory, and strategy. By developing members as both teachers and learners, the committee helps build the shared knowledge needed to understand local conditions, evaluate strategy, and connect the chapter’s campaigns to a broader socialist vision.

items.heading: Technology and Information Security Committee
items.body: The Technology and Information Security Committee maintains the digital tools and infrastructure that support DSA Fort Worth’s organizing. The committee manages systems used for chapter communications, websites, membership information, data management, and internal collaboration while promoting strong privacy, security, accessibility, and maintenance practices.

items.question: What is the difference between a working group and a committee?
items.answer: Working groups organize around political issues such as housing, immigrant justice, labor, and electoral power. Committees build the internal administrative capacity needed to sustain the chapter, including communications, political education, technology, and membership development.

items.question: How do I join a working group or committee?
items.answer: Attend an upcoming meeting or complete the chapter’s Get Involved form. You can identify the areas that interest you and a chapter organizer will help connect you with the appropriate group.

items.question: Can members propose new work?
items.answer: Yes. DSA Fort Worth members can develop ideas, organize with other members, and use the chapter’s democratic processes to propose campaigns, projects, working groups, and other initiatives.

items.question: How can I become active in the chapter?
items.answer: You can attend DSA Fort Worth 101, come to an event or meeting, or complete the Get Involved form. The Get Involved form helps us to identify and connect you to campaigns, working groups, committees, and activities that interest you. [Get Involved Form](https://fortworthdsa.solidarity.tech/get-involved-with-dsa-fort-worth).

items.question: Do I need experience to participate?
items.answer: No. Members with all levels of experience can attend meetings, learn new skills, and contribute based on their interests and capacity. Working groups and committees should help members develop and do not expect everyone to arrive as an expert.

data.title: About Us
data.lead: DSA Fort Worth is a member-funded, member-led democratic socialist organization building working-class power throughout Tarrant County.

content.heading: Building Socialist Power in Tarrant County

children.text: DSA Fort Worth is a chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, the largest socialist organization in the United States. As of 2026, DSA has more than 120,000 members nationally. Locally, we’re more than 300 members in Tarrant County.

Together, we organize for economic justice by championing housing, healthcare, strong unions, and public institutions that meet people’s needs and are building a more democratic society and economy that works for everyone.

content.heading: Democracy Should Extend to Every Part of Our Lives

children.text: Democratic socialism is the belief that people should have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape their lives. This extends past government and into our workplaces, neighborhoods, and economy.

Democratic socialists seek an economy around human needs rather than private profit. That includes expanding democratic control over essential institutions and resources, strengthening the power of workers and tenants, and ensuring that everyone has access to housing, healthcare, education, transportation, and the conditions necessary for a dignified life.
We believe ordinary people are capable of governing their communities, shaping public priorities, and making collective decisions about the institutions on which they depend.
National DSA’s Workers Deserve More program presents a shared vision organized around three broad areas:
Thriving working-class communities
A working-class foreign policy
Working-class democracy

The program includes housing and healthcare for all, labor rights, socialist feminism, an end to mass incarceration, environmental justice, opposition to U.S. military intervention, abolishing ICE, and greater democratic control of government, workplaces, and the economy.

buttons.label: Learn More About Workers Deserve More

content.heading: A Chapter Governed by Its Members

children.text: DSA Fort Worth is a democratic, member-led organization. Members in good standing collectively determine the chapter’s political direction, priorities, leadership, and use of resources.

Members exercise that authority through chapter meetings and elections. They may introduce proposals, deliberate on chapter business, vote on resolutions and endorsements, amend the bylaws, and elect chapter officers.

items.heading: Chapter General Meetings
items.body:
General meetings are the highest decision-making body of DSA Fort Worth. They provide members with a regular opportunity to receive updates, discuss chapter business, introduce proposals, and vote on decisions affecting the organization.

While open to members and supporters, voting rights are reserved for members in good standing. [To become a member, click here](https://go.dsausa.org/fort-worth-f26).

items.heading: Working Groups
items.body:
Working groups organize around specific political issues or areas of work, such as housing, electoral organizing, labor, and immigrant justice.

These bodies may research local conditions, develop proposals, organize events, recruit volunteers, and coordinate campaigns. Their work remains accountable to the chapter and the authority granted to them through chapter decisions and governing documents. [Learn more about working groups here](/our-work#working-groups).

items.heading: Committees
items.body:
Committees build and maintain the chapter’s internal organizing capacity. Their responsibilities may include communications, membership development, political education, technology and security, fundraising, and other operational needs.

Members can join committees to develop skills, contribute to chapter operations, and help create the infrastructure needed to sustain organizing over time. [Learn more about committees here](/our-work#committees).

items.heading: Campaigns
items.body:
Campaigns are coordinated efforts to achieve specific political or organizing objectives. A campaign may be developed by any member in good standing with DSA Fort Worth, proposed to, and approved by the chapter.

Campaigns translate the chapter’s political priorities into concrete action through activities such as canvassing, public education, coalition work, petitions, direct action, and engagement with public institutions. [Learn more about chapter campaigns here](/our-work#campaigns).

items.heading: Steering Committee
items.body: DSA Fort Worth’s Steering Committee is composed of ten officers elected by the chapter’s members. Together, they are responsible for maintaining the organization between chapter meetings and carrying out the duties assigned to them by the bylaws. [Learn more about our chapter structure here](/resources#bylaws).

children.text: DSA Fort Worth is committed to maintaining an organizing environment where members and participants are treated with dignity and respect. Our grievance policy provides a formal process for addressing harassment, discrimination, retaliation, violations of the Code of Conduct, and other conduct covered by the policy.
If you have a question about the grievance process or need to raise a concern, contact
DSAFortWorthHGOs@gmail.com
. Messages sent to this address are handled and managed by our chapter’s elected Harassment Grievance Officers.

items.question: What area does DSA Fort Worth serve?
items.answer: DSA Fort Worth is the Tarrant County chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America. We organize in Fort Worth and cities within Tarrant County.

items.question: How Decisions Are Made
items.answer: DSA Fort Worth is governed by its members. Members vote on chapter priorities, elect chapter leaders, and participate in decisions through the processes established in the chapter’s bylaws.

items.question: How is DSA Fort Worth funded?
items.answer: The chapter is funded by members and individual supporters. It does not rely on corporate funding. Membership dues and local donations support organizing, events, and chapter activities.

items.question: Do I need to agree with every DSA position?
items.answer: DSA is a democratic membership organization whose positions are established through member deliberation and voting. Members may hold different views about strategy and particular issues while organizing around democratically adopted priorities.

content.heading: Seeking DSA Fort Worth’s Endorsement
content.intro: Candidates interested in DSA Fort Worth’s endorsement must complete the chapter’s endorsement process.

items.heading: Application and Questionnaire
items.body: To begin the endorsement process, a candidate seeking the endorsement of DSA Fort Worth must submit an application and, shortly after, complete a candidate questionnaire.

items.heading: Engagement with Membership
items.body: Upon completing the questionnaire, it is mandatory that the candidate seeking an endorsement hold a Candidate Forum with membership prior to the general meeting where voting will take place. These meetings will be an opportunity for the candidate to introduce themselves and field questions from general membership.

items.heading: Voting
items.body: Following the Candidate Forum, a resolution to endorse the candidate will be brought up before a vote at a general meeting. An endorsement resolution will require a majority vote in favor of voters who are present to pass.

content.open_text: Submit an application to DSA Fort Worth. A representative will contact you within 14 business days to begin the endorsement process.
content.closed_text: Thank you for your interest in our endorsement. We are not accepting endorsement applications at this time. If you would like more information on our endorsement process, please reach out to [steering@dsafw.com](mailto:steering@dsafw.com).

items.question: How are chapter bylaws updated?
How do I report harassment or misconduct?
items.answer: DSA Fort Worth maintains a grievance process for reporting harm or harassment covered by the chapter’s Code of Conduct and grievance policy. Reports should be submitted through the designated grievance channel rather than the chapter’s general contact methods.

data.title: Join DSA
data.lead:
With over 120,000 members and counting, the Democratic Socialists of America is the largest socialist organization in the United States. Chapters like ours across the country are organizing together for a better world.

Upon joining DSA, you are sorted into a chapter based on where you live and gain access to membership rights like voting, proposing new work, and shaping your local chapter.

content.heading: Support DSA Fort Worth with Local Dues
content.image_brief: Marchers holding red Socialism Beats Fascism! signs

children.text: As a membership organization, dues are the backbone of our national and local operations. While national dues are required to become a member of DSA, Local dues provide a way to directly fund the work of our chapter and are a 100% contribution to DSA Fort Worth.
The Democratic Socialists of America Fort Worth is a 501(c)(4) organization. Donations are not tax-deductible.

items.question: How much does DSA membership cost?
items.answer: Members may pay monthly or annual dues, with multiple sliding scale options to meet members' financial needs. DSA also provides dues-waiver options for people experiencing financial hardship. [Dues Waiver](https://dsausa.org/dueswaiver).

items.question: Can I donate without becoming a member?
items.answer: Yes. You can make a one-time or recurring donation directly to DSA Fort Worth. Donations support local organizing but do not provide DSA membership or chapter voting rights. [Donate to DSA Fort Worth](/join#donate).

items.question: Are donations tax-deductible?
items.answer: No. DSA Fort Worth is organized as a 501(c)(4), and donations are not tax-deductible.

data.title: How to Publish a Statement, Resolution or Essay
data.summary: Everything on this page is the article template at work: the headline and summary, the hero photo, the table of contents, pull quotes, photos, and a call to action of its own. Here is how each part is made.

children.text: Articles live in the admin under News, and each one is listed on the
News page

, newest first. One template covers the chapter’s public statements, resolutions, bylaws, essays and reports, so a reader always finds the same things in the same places. Nothing below is required except a headline; a two-paragraph statement and a forty-section set of bylaws both fit.
The top of the page
The red header carries four things, all optional except the headline.
Kind: the small label above the headline (Statement, Resolution, Bylaws and so on).
Headline and summary: the summary is also what the News page, search engines and link previews show.
Date: the day a document was issued or adopted. Leave it blank to use the day you publish.
Bylines: who wrote or issued it, picked in the article’s Bylines panel. More on those below.
Hero photo: shown in full colour under the headline, and on the article’s card on the News page. Without one, the page simply starts with the text.
Writing the body
The body is a list of blocks. Most articles need only one: a Text block holding the whole piece. Add a Pull quote or Photo block wherever the text should pause, then carry on in another Text block.
Headings build the table of contents

Every Heading 2 and Heading 3 in a Text block is listed in the table of contents beside the article, and each gets its own link, so you can send someone straight to a section. For bylaws, use Heading 2 for each article and Heading 3 for each section.

The table of contents follows the reader: the red line and marker show how far down the page they are, and the current section is highlighted. On a phone it folds into a bar under the header. An article with fewer than two headings has no table of contents at all.
Quoting a source
To quote a document or a person at length, use the Quote style inside the text. It reads as a quotation, not as a headline:
Democratic socialists believe that both the economy and society should be run democratically, to meet public needs, not to make profits for a few.

body.quote: A pull quote repeats the one line you want a skimming reader to leave with.

children.text: Pull quotes and photos

A pull quote is its own block: type the line, and add who said it if it needs saying. Photos can go in two ways. A Photo block sets a picture across the column with a caption. Inside a Text block, the editor’s image button drops a picture between paragraphs.
Either way, write alt text for every photo. Describe what is in the picture for someone who can’t see it.

body.caption: A Photo block, with its caption. Photos keep their own shape; nothing is cropped.

children.text: Bylines

A byline is a profile under Bylines in the admin: a name, and optionally a short bio, a picture and a website. It can be a person or a body of the chapter, such as the Steering Committee. Make the profile once, then credit it on any article from that article’s Bylines panel.

Credits show under the headline and on the News page. Any byline with a bio or a picture also gets a short introduction at the end of the article. An article can carry several, each with a role if it helps: Photographer, Translator, Editor.
The call to action

Each article ends with a red band. Give it a heading, a sentence or two, and up to two buttons, and it becomes this article’s own ask: sign the petition the statement is about, come to the meeting where the resolution will be voted on, read the full document on another site. A button can point anywhere, on this site or off it.
Leave the heading blank and the article ends with the same Get involved band as every other page.
Before you publish
Read the summary on its own. Would it make sense in a search result?
Check the table of contents. If a heading there wouldn’t help a reader find their way, it should be bold text instead.
Open the preview on a phone.
This page is a sample. Once the first real article is up, delete it from News.
